headlines.title: Iran says two tankers have hit Hormuz naval mines, attacks regional targets in retaliation to U.S. strikes
headlines.summary: Well now, when somebody starts dropping naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz — through which, as the Energy Secretary kindly reminded us, some 17 million barrels of oil pass on a quiet Monday — you don't need a weathervane to know which way the wind is blowing for energy prices, bond yields, and the general disposition of stock markets worldwide. This is the kind of development that, like a late frost on the Nebraska corn crop, touches nearly everything at once: oil above $90 pressures airlines, raises input costs for manufacturers, stokes the inflation that keeps the Fed's hand away from the rate-cut lever, and sends bond yields climbing in a way that JPMorgan's own Grace Peters warns could put equities at serious risk if the 10-year touches 5%. Energy stocks may find a friend here, but the broad market — particularly rate-sensitive growth names — is sitting in the path of a very stiff headwind.

headlines.title: 10-year U.S. Treasury yield hits highest level since November 2023 as global bond sell-off continues
headlines.summary: Now, I've watched a good many bond markets in my time, and I'll tell you that when the 10-year Treasury yield climbs to its highest perch since late 2023 — with Japan's 10-year simultaneously crossing 3% for the first time in a generation and European gilts joining the rout — that's not a local squall, that's a system moving across the whole prairie. Rising yields tighten financial conditions for every borrower from the U.S. government on down to the young couple trying to afford a home on an adjustable-rate mortgage, and they make the earnings yields on stocks look a good deal less appetizing by comparison. The Fed's September meeting is now firmly in play as a potential hike, which would be the sort of surprise that tends to separate the patient investor from the fellow who bought on margin.

headlines.title: Nvidia Nears $14 Billion Deal to Buy Hugging Face | The Pulse 9/2/2026
headlines.summary: A $14 billion acquisition by the most consequential semiconductor company of this era is the sort of thing that, as my old friend Charlie might say, concentrates the mind wonderfully — both for Nvidia shareholders and for every AI-adjacent company that suddenly finds itself either a potential partner or a potential competitor of a firm that now controls not just the picks and shovels of the AI gold rush, but the map of the mine itself. Hugging Face is the central marketplace for open-source AI models, meaning this deal touches the ambitions of every hyperscaler, every enterprise software company, and every startup that has been building on top of freely available models; it also raises the sort of antitrust questions that tend to keep lawyers employed and regulators animated for years. I'd watch NVDA, GOOGL, META, and MSFT for the ripples — and I'd watch the open-source AI community for the reaction, which may prove louder than the deal price suggests.
